lines.content: description: Apply the SE-EDU Git commit message convention when proposing, writing, or reviewing a commit message in this project. Covers subject line mood, capitalisation and length, body wrapping, and what the body must explain. Use before every commit made in this repository.
Apply this to every commit message written in this project.
- Use the **imperative mood**: `Add README.md`, `Move index.html file to root`.
Not `Added README.md`, not `Adding README.md`. A useful test: the subject
should complete the sentence *"If applied, this commit will ..."*.
- Keep it to **50 characters**; 72 is the hard limit.
- An optional prefix naming the scope or category is allowed, for example
`Person class: Remove static imports` or `chore: Update release date`.
- Separate the subject from the body with **one blank line**.
- Separate paragraphs with blank lines; use bullet points where they help.
- Explain **what** and **why**, not **how**. The reader should be able to judge
whether the change is a good idea without reading the diff.
- Do not repeat information already given in code comments.
1. the current situation, in the present tense,
3. what this commit does about it, in the imperative,
4. why that approach, and any other detail worth recording.
Existing history uses a capitalised category prefix, which the standard permits.
Keep using it, and keep it consistent with what is already in the log:
| `Refactor:` | A change to structure that keeps behaviour identical |
| `Docs:` | Documentation, header comments, agent files, skills |
Check the recent log with `git log --oneline -20` before choosing a prefix, so a
new commit matches the vocabulary already in use.
- One commit does **one** thing. If the subject needs the word "and", or the
body has to describe two unrelated changes, split the commit.
- Keep changes to code separate from standalone changes to agent files, skills,
Refactor: Parenthesise the command keyword match
findCommandType decides whether an input line starts a command by
combining an exact keyword match with a prefix match, written as
`a || b && c`. The condition is correct only because && binds tighter
than ||, which a reader has to know and check.
Add parentheses around the && operands so the grouping is explicit.
The coding standard asks for parentheses whenever && and || are mixed,
and the shorter grouped line also drops under the 110 character soft
- Propose the message and check it against the rules above.
- Verify the subject: imperative, capitalised, no full stop, within 50/72.
- Verify the body wraps at 72 characters.
- Never commit or push unless the user has explicitly asked for it.

Covers naming, layout, line length, wrapping, braces, statements, imports, and Javadoc header comments. Use for any Java file in this repository.
This project follows the **basic + intermediate** levels of the standard. Apply
every rule below to Java code you write, edit, or review here. When a rule and an
existing local convention conflict, follow the rule and fix the surrounding code
only if the fix is in scope.
- All names are in **English**, using American spelling.

- Name length tracks scope: wide scope gets a descriptive name; a scratch or
A bare verb such as `matches` is not acceptable for a boolean variable; use
- Line length: **soft limit 110 characters, hard limit 120**. Stay under 110.

- Keep a method or constructor name attached to its opening parenthesis.
- Prefer a higher-level break over a lower-level one.
- A ternary is either on one line, or split across three with the operators
- Braces use **K&R style**: the opening brace ends the statement line, the
closing brace starts its own line. `else`, `catch` and `finally` continue the
line of the preceding closing brace.
- Separate logical units inside a block with **one blank line**.
- Surround binary operators with spaces: `a = (b + c) * d;`
- Space after each comma: `doSomething(a, b, c, d);`
- Space after each semicolon in a `for` header: `for (i = 0; i < 10; i++)`
- Import order must be consistent, each group separated by a blank line:
- Attach the array specifier to the type: `int[] a`, not `int a[]`.
- Declare variables in the **smallest possible scope** and initialise them where
- Class variables are **never public**; constants are the exception.
- **Always brace** the body of a loop or conditional, even a single statement:
- Put the condition on a separate line from the action.
- In a traditional `switch`, a `case` that deliberately falls through must carry
a `// Fallthrough` comment. Arrow form (`case ABC -> ...`) needs no comment.

This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* IDE and level of expertise: VSC, Advanced
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.

mandatory, not advisory: a change that does not comply is not finished.
Non-compliant code found while working on something else may be corrected in the
same change when the fix is small and in scope; otherwise leave it and say so.
After each code update, complete both steps before handing the work back to the user:
1. Review `test/ui-test-plan.md` and update it when the change affects UI behaviour, coverage, inputs, or expected output. Do not rewrite expected output merely to conceal a regression.

2. Invoke the project-specific `$test-ui` skill to run the UI test plan. If a case fails, report its recorded input plus expected and actual output; the skill stops the test session at the first failure.
Maintain JUnit tests for approximately the top 50% of methods by testing value. Prioritize complex, core, and
critical business logic over trivial accessors and boilerplate. After every code change, review the affected JUnit
tests and update or extend them as needed to continue meeting this target. Run the complete JUnit test suite before
handing the work back to the user.
All commit messages in this project must follow the SE-EDU Git convention
Invoke the project-specific `seedu-git-standard` skill before proposing or
writing any commit message. This is mandatory for all future commits.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.
